newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya drafting bill for anti-graft authority.
newsitem.headline: Kenya drafting bill for anti-graft authority.

text.p: Kenya is drafting a bill to set up an anti-graft authority after the International Monetary Fund threatened to drop an aid package unless measures were taken this week.

The independent Daily Nation newspaper on Tuesday quoted Attorney-General Amos Wako as saying he was drafting a bill to set up an authority to investigate corruption by individuals with political links.

He said the draft bill would be incorporated in another bill promised by President Daniel arap Moi's government calling for the amendment or repeal of 11 laws which the opposition demands be scrapped as repressive before a general election this year.
But the latest in the flurry of law drafting did little to impress opposition leaders campaigning for political reforms that would cut the power of Moi, 73 and president for 19 years.

"It is highly unlikely that any anti-corruption commission will have any teeth because if it did the first thing it would have to bite is the people setting it up," Richard Leakey, a leader of the unregistered Safina party, told Reuters.

Moi's government blunted an opposition-backed rally in the Indian Ocean city of Mombasa at the weekend by licensing it after clashes elsewhere in June and July between police and pro-reform demonstrators rattled foreign investors and tourists.
Wako said he preferred a comprehensive law against economic crimes but it would take too long to prepare. "I'm moving fast to draft a bill for the cabinet to consider," he said.
The IMF, warning Kenya to make its much-criticised public sector more accountable, said last Thursday a big IMF loan package would lapse unless the government acted by July 31.
The IMF extended a three-year Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) loan worth $205 million in April last year but payments were conditional on Kenya meeting promises to change.

The last scheduled ESAF payment, a $36 million tranche, was delayed by the IMF for a month until July 31, partly because of concern at the way Kenyan authorities handled the multi-million dollar Goldenberg International financial scandal.

Asked if the government would meet the IMF deadline of July 31, Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi said: "We will respond to them before their deadline. Losing the money would be a big blow to our economic programme and could affect growth."
"The government does not condone abuse of public office or corruption in the public sector and is doing all it can to reduce, and possibly eradicate, it," Mudavadi told Reuters.
"Obviously the government is desperate to hold on to the ESAF," Leakey said. "I hope the IMF and international donor community will not fall for this sort of seduction."
He said the government clearly felt under domestic and international pressure and was drafting laws "thick and fast".
The IMF hit out in June at the government failure to act decisively to "ensure transparency and accountability in the use of public funds and resolve outstanding energy sector reform".
Crispus Muititu, permanent secretary in the Energy Ministry, said on Monday a bill was being drafted for an independent regulatory board. Mudavadi said it was part of the IMF issues.
IMF officials said earlier this month the IMF wanted the government to clarify what it planned to do to counter "irregularities" that made the Goldenberg scandal possible.
Goldenberg International was paid about $100 million by the government in 1992 under an export scheme for gold and diamond exports. Kenya produces very little gold and no diamonds.
The IMF delayed releasing the $36 million ESAF tranche after the high court decided on June 20 to end the prosecution of a businessman and former officials implicated in the scandal.
Wako has charged the businessman and former officials again.
The opposition had cited alleged links to powerful Kenyan politicians as the main reason the prosecution was dropped.
